claims.text: Q235 is a low-carbon structural steel.
As-received Q235 has only a thin, minimal native oxide layer before thermal treatment.
The composition and integrity of the oxide passivation film govern the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
High-temperature annealing of Q235 steel in air can form a predominantly dense, adherent Fe2O3-rich surface film.
A dense Fe2O3-rich film on Q235 acts as a barrier to ion transport and elemental dissolution during molten-salt exposure.
A porous or mixed Fe2O3/Fe3O4 film is less protective than a dense Fe2O3-rich film.
Porous or mixed iron-oxide films permit salt penetration and accelerate active oxidation and corrosion.
Dense Cr2O3-containing passivation films provide corrosion resistance in stainless steels, Fe-Cr alloys, and several Cr-containing HEAs.
Passivation-film composition or enrichment is associated with corrosion behavior in HEAs and Fe-Cr alloys.
Elemental dissolution during molten-salt exposure can produce measurable mass loss and near-surface elemental depletion.
Annealed Q235 specimens having a dense Fe2O3-rich film will show lower mass loss than as-received or mixed-oxide specimens during exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealed Q235 specimens having a dense Fe2O3-rich film will retain more hardness during molten-salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 specimens having a dense Fe2O3-rich film will exhibit less elemental dissolution than as-received or mixed-oxide specimens.
As-received Q235 will undergo moderate corrosion and greater mass loss and degradation than protected annealed specimens under high-temperature salt attack.
The proposed oxide-film mechanism applies primarily when 700–900 °C molten-salt conditions permit oxide formation or transformation.
At room temperature or during non-salt exposure, atmospheric or other corrosion mechanisms may dominate instead of the proposed high-temperature oxide-film mechanism.

The governing cause can be tested by comparing air-annealed Q235 with as-received Q235 under otherwise identical molten-salt exposure and measuring oxide composition, morphology, mass change, hardness, and elemental distribution.
Failure of dense Fe2O3-rich specimens to show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion or damage relative to the controls would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
